pr_comments:
The implementation looks good to me now, however my concerns about this potentially regressing performance because we're adding a `try`/`catch` in the hot path still remain. Performance of the serializer has historically been very sensitive to changes made in this location, so I'd want to see a run of the benchmark suite against the change before I could sign off on it.

Given that this change is made to address a hypothetical bug that nobody has actually has reported (Disposable IEnumerators are largely legacy and if they do exist chances are users would be better off using `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` which does handle disposal correctly).

I'm going to close this PR for now and the related issue, thank you for taking the time to work on this!

> Disposable IEnumerators are largely legacy

Not disputing the rest of your comment, but can you elaborate on this? Any C# iterator with a try/finally is going to have a meaningful IDisposable.Dispose.
I wasn't aware of that use case. It definitely adds more points in favor of us doing this, but we still need to run the benchmarks against the change.

Ok, let's see if we can get this merged. I rebased the branch and pushed a change the removes the need for new `try`/`catch` clauses in the hot path. I ran the microbenchmark suite and detected no change in performance.

issue_context.title: System.Text.Json not properly disposing enumerators on exceptions
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @eiriktsarpalis, @layomia See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
Related to #48322 and #46349. The current IEnumerable converters don't dispose of enumerators in certain scenaria where nested element converters throw exceptions. Reproducing test (using a few System.Text.Json.Tests components): ```csharp [Fact] public static void WriteIEnumerableT_ElementSerializationThrows_DisposesEnumerators() { var items = new RefCountedList>(Enumerable.Repeat(ThrowingEnumerable(), 1)); Assert.Throws(() => JsonSerializer.Serialize(items.AsEnumerable())); Assert.Equal(0, items.RefCount); // items.RefCount evaluates to 1 static IEnumerable ThrowingEnumerable() { yield return 42; throw new DivideByZeroException(); } } ``` Note that #50778 makes changes to the serialization infrastructure to handle IEnumerator disposal in the async case, however changes on the individual converter level will still need to be made. cc @layomia @steveharter.
Author: eiriktsarpalis
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Text.Json`
Milestone: 6.0.0
Suggest moving to 7.0. No community asks that I'm aware of.
Note that this should be fixed for Dictionary converters as well.
Moving to Future, as we won't have time to work on this in the .NET 7 timeframe.
After deliberation we've decided to not fix this bug. It is largely a theoretical concern that no user has reported so far.

review_comments: Because this is now setting the enumerator early on, you should probably remove the assignments happening later in the same method bodies.
Might be worth checking if this early assignment could break invariants elsewhere in the serializer (look for possible locations where `CollectionEnumerator is null` is being checked)

I have cleaned up these duplicate assignments.
Unfortunately, the enumerator for the `DictionaryOfTKeyTValueConverter` class  has the `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>.Enumerator` type which a _value type_. I have changed it to `IEnumerator<KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>>` to work with a _reference type_ but my first performance tests reveal that it introduces some noticeable performance regressions :/
Do you have any idea how to tackle this issue?

---

I have not found any broken invariant for `CollectionEnumerator`.

In most built-in collections and compiler generated iterators the dispose method is a no-op anyway. Perhaps it makes sense to precompute whether that is the case and only store the `CollectionEnumerator` early if found to be a custom enumerator or an enumerator known to have dispose logic.
Ok, I have removed the early assignment in the `DictionaryOfTKeyTValueConverter` class as it is the only one in such a situation.

I don't think that would work here, the `TCollection` could be any IDictionary type which may or may not have a disposable enumerator. It might make sense to just check against a list of known types, although that would probably require new API for the case of the source generator.

In any case, a fix seems to be creating more problems than what it is solving :-(

Here `TCollection` inherits from `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` where the `GetEnumerator()` method is _not_ virtual, so I would not expect any issue.
Do I miss something?
TDictionary inherits from IEnumerable, not Dictionary. The enumerator may or may not require disposal.

Oh, I think we do not talk about the same converter here.
The enumerator disposal is now correctly handled (i.e. even in case of exception) for all converters _except_ for the [`DictionaryOfTKeyTValueConverter`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a2861f397ebbc68047692fed9032f36b414ef84d/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Converters/Collection/DictionaryOfTKeyTValueConverter.cs#L13) one, where we can safely ignore the disposal of the enumerator as it  is implemented as a [no-op](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c1a4c9c48f215547679b49f8e2fce5077a63f945/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/Dictionary.cs#L1418) and cannot be overridden.

> where we can safely ignore the disposal of the enumerator as it is implemented as a [no-op](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c1a4c9c48f215547679b49f8e2fce5077a63f945/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Collections/Generic/Dictionary.cs#L1418) and cannot be overridden.

That's not quite true, the converter applies to types inheriting from Dictionary which may or may not be implementing disposal semantics in the enumerator.
Are these three converters the only ones accessing the `CollectionEnumerator` field?
No, I have now aligned all of them to the new pattern even if their enumerator is not inheriting from `IDisposable`.
